“Allow insecure” cannot skip certificate checks in this core — it only verifies the certificate against the SNI instead of the address. Set an SNI, or paste the certificate’s SHA-256 into the pinned certificate field; a self-signed certificate can only be trusted by pinning it.

Sets the system proxy on GNOME, KDE, Windows or macOS. Browsers and most apps follow it, and no administrator rights are needed. This is the default.
Only opens a local SOCKS and HTTP proxy on 127.0.0.1 and changes nothing else. Point each app at it yourself.
Sends every app through a virtual network adapter, including apps that ignore the system proxy. Asks for administrator rights each time you connect. Tor and Psiphon keep using the system proxy.
Built on the Xray core, with Psiphon, Tor, Snowflake, obfs4, Conjure, DNSTT, VayDNS, MasterDNS, AmneziaWG, OpenConnect and IKEv2.
The core that carries your traffic is built on open-source projects licensed under GPL-3.0, LGPL-3.0 and MPL-2.0. Our patched sources are published, as those licences require.

A short, accurate summary — the full document is online
No account. No backend of ours. No analytics.
A client, not a VPN service
ZedSecure connects to servers, subscriptions and networks that you add. We operate none of them, and your traffic never reaches us.
Configurations, credentials, settings, statistics and logs live in the app's private storage and are removed when you uninstall. Vault configurations are encrypted with AES-256-GCM.
The app contains no analytics, telemetry, crash reporting, advertising or tracking libraries, and there is no account to identify you by.

The location lookup, the speed test (Cloudflare), routing-rule downloads (GitHub), the update check (the Play listing) and your chosen DNS or Tor infrastructure each connect out — and each necessarily sees your IP address.
The per-app proxy reads your installed apps only to show you the list. It is read on the device and never transmitted; only your selection is saved.
The identifier shown in Settings is Android's ANDROID_ID. The app never sends it anywhere — it exists so someone can bind a locked Vault config to your device if you choose to give it to them.
A rooted or compromised device offers no guarantees. Your privacy also depends on the provider you chose, and a VPN changes where your traffic appears from — it does not make you anonymous.

The fastest server in the group carries new connections. If it stops answering, the connections that hit it continue on the next server within a second or two, and Auto stays there until a clearly faster server turns up — so your address does not keep changing.
